outputs.L1:
**After Hasior**

They fired a bullet into the head of each question, trying to kill Kant’s unending argument with Hegel. They burned laws, moral codes, and the Golden Means. Anyone who served tea and cookies to Death—anyone who looked or acted as though he knew love—stood before the firing squad. All questions had to go, pronoun or noun. If one crawled on shattered kneecaps, whimpering and begging for mercy, it was still half a question.

* * *

The little skyscraper of glass boxes outside Zakopane, struck by sunlight at a certain angle at the same time each day, looks like condos where nimble ghosts still stand against the darkest answers. No, I can’t hear a single voice pleading. But I do hear gusts coming down from the hills. No, you’re wrong again. The crow perched on the totem is real. Look at how the light lifts from its wings. But I wish I could understand what it is trying to say. I think I heard a name.
outputs.L2:
**After Hasior**

They put a round through every question’s skull, hoping to silence Kant’s endless dispute with Hegel. Statutes, ethical rules, and the Golden Means went up in flames. Whoever offered Death tea and biscuits—whoever seemed, in appearance or behavior, to understand love—was marched before the rifles. Every question, whether pronoun or noun, had to be erased. Even one dragging itself along on shattered knees, sobbing and asking to be spared, remained half a question.

* * *

Beyond Zakopane, the small high-rise built from glass compartments catches the sun each day at the same hour and angle. It resembles condominiums where agile spirits continue resisting the blackest answers. No, I hear no single voice begging. What reaches me instead are blasts of wind descending from the hills. No—you are mistaken once more. The crow sitting atop the totem truly exists. Watch the light rise from its feathers. Still, I wish I knew what it was trying to tell me. I believe I heard someone’s name.
outputs.L3:
The poem imagines a world in which questions are violently destroyed, as though uncertainty itself were an enemy. By eliminating every form of inquiry, the poem evokes an extreme attempt to put an end to philosophical debate, doubt, and the search for meaning. This rejection extends beyond questions to laws, moral codes, moderation, and even expressions of love. Nothing that might guide, restrain, or humanize thought is allowed to remain.

Even weakened, partial, or unfinished questions are treated as dangerous. Their mere existence threatens the desire for absolute certainty, so they too must be eliminated. Against this atmosphere of intellectual and moral destruction, the poem introduces a striking image: a sunlit glass structure near Zakopane, seemingly haunted by ghosts that resist dark or oppressive answers. The brightness and transparency of the setting contrast with the threatening certainty imposed elsewhere.

In the final movement, the speaker turns toward the natural world. They hear its sounds and encounter a real crow, but this apparent contact with reality does not resolve the poem’s uncertainty. The crow may be delivering a message—or even speaking a name—yet the speaker cannot determine what was said or what it means. Thus, despite the effort to destroy all questions, ambiguity survives. The poem ultimately suggests that uncertainty cannot be erased, because even the most immediate experiences continue to invite interpretation.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a world in which abstract thought is subjected to a violent, almost grotesque attack. Its surreal imagery turns philosophical inquiry into a physical struggle: questions are assaulted, moral principles are damaged, and ideas such as love and meaning seem vulnerable to force. The references to Kant and Hegel evoke philosophical systems that seek to explain experience through reason, ethics, and historical development. Yet, within the poem, these systems no longer offer security. They appear exposed to destruction or appropriation, as though someone were trying to silence uncertainty by imposing a final, authoritative answer.

The allusion to Władysław Hasior’s art reinforces this atmosphere. Hasior’s assemblages and monuments often combine ordinary materials, religious or patriotic symbols, fire, metal, glass, and elements of the natural landscape. They can seem ceremonial and unsettling at the same time. By invoking his work, the poem places philosophy within a similarly charged artistic space, where beauty and violence, reverence and mockery, creation and destruction coexist. The assault is therefore not only directed at particular thinkers or concepts. It threatens the very possibility of asking what is true, what is good, what love means, and whether human life possesses any stable significance.

Nevertheless, the poem does not allow violence to have the final word. The glass sculpture remains fragile, luminous, and difficult to interpret. Glass can be shattered, but it can also reflect and refract light, producing new perspectives rather than a single fixed image. The mountain gusts introduce a force that cannot be controlled by philosophical systems or ideological commands. Light likewise suggests revelation without delivering a complete explanation: it makes things visible while preserving shadows and ambiguity. Even the crow, often associated with death, warning, or dark intelligence, resists being reduced to one symbolic meaning. Its presence keeps the scene open and unsettled.

These elements preserve an irreducible mystery at the center of the poem. Human beings may attempt to settle philosophical and moral questions through argument, authority, or violence, but art and nature continue to disrupt such certainty. The sculpture changes with the light; the wind moves through the landscape; the crow observes, interrupts, or calls out without translating its message into a clear doctrine. Together, they suggest that meaning cannot simply be imposed from above.

The poem therefore moves between destruction and endurance. It portrays an attack on philosophy, morality, love, and meaning, yet it also shows that questioning survives. Art does not provide a neat solution, and nature does not answer in human language. Instead, both preserve the openness from which genuine thought begins. Even when someone claims to possess the final answer, the world continues to reflect, shift, sound, and resist. Mystery remains—not as a failure of understanding, but as the condition that keeps interpretation, imagination, and philosophical inquiry alive.
outputs.L5: After seeing Władysław Hasior’s striking sculptures and assemblages, visitors often remember their unusual mix of everyday objects, religious symbols, and folk traditions. Hasior transformed discarded materials into expressive works filled with drama and emotion. They challenge viewers to reconsider the boundaries between art, memory, and ordinary life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem titled “After Hasior,” inspired by Polish sculptor Władysław Hasior, blending philosophy, violence, death, glass architecture, Zakopane, ghosts, wind, and a crow.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Hasior

In Zakopane, the mountains keep their verdict behind their teeth. Snow enters the town dressed as ash, and the wind, that old smuggler, carries iron spoons, burnt dolls, cavalry songs, the red thread of a severed banner. Nothing arrives intact. Even daylight has been hammered thin.

A glass house stands where the road forgets its name. Its walls are transparent, yet no one can see through them. Inside, chairs kneel around a table set for the dead. Each plate contains a small black flame. Philosophy sits at the head, polishing a mirror with a butcher’s apron, asking whether the wound is a door or merely the memory of a door.

No one answers.

The ghosts have gone out to graze among the pines. They wear medals made from bottle caps and halos cut from rusted saws. One carries his skull under his arm like a loaf of bread. Another presses an ear to the earth and hears the future loading its rifle.

Above them, a crow nails its shadow to the sky.

Violence does not enter suddenly. It has always been here: in the axe sleeping inside the tree, in the window rehearsing its shattering, in the immaculate geometry of the glass pavilion. When the wind rises, the whole building becomes an instrument. It plays with the voices of those who died unnamed—high notes of mothers, low notes of soldiers, the thin metallic cry of a child’s abandoned sled.

By morning, blood has turned to red wool tied around the antlers of a wooden saint. Death, embarrassed by its own seriousness, hides beneath a carnival mask. The crow descends and pecks once at the frozen ground.

A bell rings without a church.

The Tatras lean closer.

And for one impossible moment, everything broken—bayonet, angel, chimney, bone—casts the same bright shadow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental ekphrastic poem responding to a Hasior artwork. Use fragmentary imagery, personify questions, reference Kant and Hegel, and end with a mysterious name heard in a crow’s call.
counterfactuals.output:
**Black Landscape, After Hasior**

A field assembled from after:

char,  
wire,  
a spoon dreaming it was a moon,  
the torn uniform of weather.

Questions enter barefoot.  
One lifts the rusted blade and asks, *Whose harvest?*  
Another crouches beside the scorched doll,  
warming its hands at the absence of fire.

Kant stands at the frame’s cold border—  
the sublime buttoned to his throat—  
insisting terror must keep its distance.

But Hegel has already climbed inside:  
history with a hammer,  
history nesting in the helmet,  
history turning each black feather  
into its opposite  
and back again.

No sky. Only its iron receipt.

A wheel remembers horses.  
A cross forgets God.  
The trumpet, packed with soil,  
raises a mute red anthem.

Then the questions grow faces.  
Then the faces become locks.  
Then every lock opens  
onto the same burned hill.

From somewhere beyond the gallery  
a crow nails one syllable to another—

**Ka—zimir.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, dreamlike prose poem in which a totalitarian firing squad tries to eliminate every question, followed by a vision of sunlit glass boxes near Zakopane inhabited by ghosts.
counterfactuals.output:
At midnight the Ministry led the questions into the courtyard.

They came barefoot, blinking in the snow: *Why?* with its broken spectacles, *Who?* clutching a photograph, *Where?* still smelling of pine and railway smoke. Even *When?*, the youngest, had been dragged from its bed. The soldiers arranged them against the wall beneath a clock whose hands had been removed.

The commandant read the sentence: uncertainty was treason; wonder, sabotage; doubt, a door left open to the weather.

“Ready.”

The rifles lifted.

*Is there another world?* asked a small voice.

“Fire.”

Black birds burst from the wall. The questions fell, but their shadows remained standing. All night the squad fired into those shadows, then into the echoes, then into the mouths of the soldiers themselves. By dawn no one could remember what had been forbidden. The clock ticked without hands. Snow covered the courtyard like a page no one dared to read.

Years later—or perhaps the same morning—I saw, near Zakopane, a field of glass boxes shining under the Tatras.

Sunlight entered them and could not leave.

Inside each box lived a ghost. Some sat at transparent tables, lifting empty cups. Some combed the hair of vanished children. One pressed its face to the glass and fogged it with the breath of a century. Another held a question carefully in both hands, as if warming a wounded bird.

The mountains watched in their blue sleep. Bells drifted up from the valley. The glass boxes blazed brighter and brighter, until the ghosts seemed made not of death but of imprisoned daylight.

Then every question opened its eyes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poetic meditation on Władysław Hasior using ampersands, abrupt denials, philosophical allusions, and uncanny images of tea with Death, busted kneecaps, mountain gusts, a totem, and a real crow.
counterfactuals.output:
**HASIOR, AFTER THE WEATHER**

Not monument. No.  
A wound learning carpentry.

He gathers the century’s roadside glitter—  
fork & feather, axle & saint,  
the burnt spoon dreaming itself silver—  
& teaches debris to stand upright  
against the tribunal of usefulness.

In Zakopane, a mountain gust  
cross-examines the pines.  
The peaks refuse transcendence.  
Kant loses his footing.  
Nietzsche comes down with busted kneecaps,  
still muttering *height, height*,  
while history drags its tin halo  
through the snow.

Not beauty. No.  
Beauty has grease under its nails.

At dusk Hasior pours tea for Death  
from a cracked enamel pot.  
Death takes sugar, then another,  
embarrassed by the ordinary spoon.  
Between them: a silence  
with the texture of scorched velvet,  
a small flag trembling in no nation.

Outside, the totem wakes—  
wire ribs, wooden tongue,  
a bicycle wheel where the sun should be.  
It does not represent.  
It watches.

& on its shoulder—  
not symbol, not omen,  
not the black punctuation of the soul—

a real crow,

hopping once,  
cocking its mineral eye  
toward our bright republic of wreckage,

then lifting into the mountain gust  
with one stolen button  
shining in its beak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a two-part avant-garde poem that moves from the execution of morality and inquiry to a quieter mountainous scene where light strikes a glass structure and the speaker struggles to interpret a crow’s message.
counterfactuals.output:
### I. Public Works

At noon they brought Morality out  
in a coat stitched from verdicts.

Inquiry followed—  
barefoot, carrying a small, illegal question  
between her teeth.

The square had been scrubbed of ambiguity.  
Officials adjusted the horizon.  
A bell rehearsed its one iron syllable.

First, Morality was made to kneel  
before the machine of perfect reasons.  
Then Inquiry, still asking *by whom?*  
was hooded with an answer.

Two trapdoors opened.

The crowd applauded in straight lines.

Afterward, the executioner washed his hands  
in a basin labeled **FACT**,  
and every mirror in the city  
was promoted to judge.

Night entered through the wound  
without papers.



### II. Mountain Grammar

Higher up, snow keeps no minutes.

A glass house stands on the ridge—  
almost absent,  
a thought the mountain has not decided  
whether to think.

Dawn strikes it.

For one bright second  
the whole structure becomes a bell  
made only of light,  
ringing without sound  
into the pines.

A crow lands on the transparent roof.

It knocks once.  
Then twice.

Black beak, black cipher—  
a telegram from the executed, perhaps,  
or merely hunger  
wearing its oldest uniform.

I listen until listening becomes weather.

The crow says: **stone**.  
Or **go**.  
Or **there is no word for what survives us**.

Below, the valleys fill with blue silence.

The bird opens its wings,  
and I cannot tell  
whether the message has departed  
or begun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
